name: Tibetan Empire
summary: An empire of the Tibetan plateau under the Yarlung kings. At its height it reached Chang’an and Central Asia, and it brought Buddhism to Tibet.

knownFor.label: Tibetan script
knownFor.note: Traditionally created under Songtsen Gampo to translate Buddhist texts.

knownFor.label: Jokhang temple
knownFor.note: Lhasa’s holiest temple, founded in the 7th century.

knownFor.label: Treaty pillar (821–823)
knownFor.note: A stone pillar recording peace with Tang China.

knownFor.label: Samye Monastery
knownFor.note: The first Buddhist monastery in Tibet.

location.value: The Tibetan plateau, reaching into Central Asia, China, Nepal and India.

terrain.value: The high Tibetan Plateau, the Yarlung valley and passes into Central Asia, China and India.
terrain.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

climate.value: Cold and dry at high altitude; farming only in sheltered valleys.
climate.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

resources.value: Yak and sheep herds, barley, horses and gold.
resources.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

disasters.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

population.value: Perhaps about 10 million in the 8th century (a rough estimate).

urbanisation.value: Lhasa became the capital in the 7th century.

disease.value: Smallpox epidemics are recorded in Tibetan and Chinese sources.
disease.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

migration.value: Unknown in detail; Tibetan garrisons settled in conquered regions.
migration.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

economicBase.value: Herding and barley farming, plus tribute and control of Silk Road routes.
economicBase.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

tradeRoutes.value: Controlled parts of the Silk Road, including Dunhuang (787–848).
tradeRoutes.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

moneyAndTax.value: Little is known; taxes were paid in goods and military service.
moneyAndTax.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

inequality.value: Powerful noble clans held land and office.
inequality.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

governmentType.value: Monarchy (tsenpo) with powerful ministers from noble clans.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Tibetan Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

keyRulers.value: Songtsen Gampo (618–650), Trisong Detsen (753–797), Tritsuk Detsen (815–838).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Yarlung dynasty; ministers often ruled for young kings.
succession.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

institutions.value: Military-administrative “horns” (ru) that organised soldiers and land.
institutions.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

stability.value: Assassinations in 838 and 842 ended the empire.

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between Buddhist and Bön factions at court.
eliteConflict.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

armyAndTech.value: Large armies of armoured cavalry; Tibetan chain mail was admired by Chinese writers.
armyAndTech.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

majorWars.value: Wars with Tang China; Tibetan troops occupied the Tang capital Chang’an briefly in 763.
majorWars.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

territoryChange.value: Perhaps about 4.6 million km² around 800, the largest extent.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival: Tang China; treaties of 783 and 821–823.

inventions.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

scienceEducation.value: Large-scale translation of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit.
scienceEducation.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

openness.value: Adopted Buddhism and learning from India and China.
openness.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

religion.value: Bon and older beliefs, with Buddhism promoted by the kings, especially Trisong Detsen.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Tibetan Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

languageWriting.value: Old Tibetan, written in a script traditionally credited to Songtsen Gampo’s minister Thonmi Sambhota.
languageWriting.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

artsArchitecture.value: Samye Monastery (8th century), the Jokhang temple and inscribed stone pillars.
artsArchitecture.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

socialStructure.value: Kings, noble clans, Buddhist monks (later), herders and farmers.
socialStructure.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the divine king and, later, Buddhism.
sharedIdentity.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

neighbours.value: Tang China, Nanzhao, the Uyghurs, the Abbasid Caliphate and Indian kingdoms.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Tibetan Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

ideasReligions.value: Buddhist texts were translated from Sanskrit and Chinese; Tibetan Buddhism took shape.
ideasReligions.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

colonisation.value: None overseas; it ruled conquered lands directly or through vassals.
colonisation.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

riseSignals.value: Songtsen Gampo united the Tibetan clans and moved the capital to Lhasa.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Tibetan Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

peakPeriod.value: Under Trisong Detsen (753–797), when Tibet briefly took Chang’an (763).
peakPeriod.source: Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

declineSignals.value: Rivalry between Buddhist and Bon factions and the killing of kings in 838 and 842.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Tibetan Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (1987)

sources.value: Old Tibetan Annals, Chinese sources. Checked against Wikipedia (“Tibetan Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Old Tibetan Annals and Chinese records agree on major events; the end date is 842 or 848.
